cards.explanation: The answer is spring, friends. The prophet tells Ahab, Israel's king, “Go and strengthen your position, and take note what you must do, for in the spring the king of Aram will come up against you.” That's a warning with a season stamped right on it. Then verse 26 rolls around and Ben-hadad, Aram's king, shows up on schedule.

The answer is the plains, friends. Ben-hadad's servants say, “Their gods are gods of the hills. That is why they prevailed over us.” So they say they should fight on the plains, where they think they will surely prevail. They've got a whole plan built on that idea.

The answer is an army just like the one he lost. The servants say to raise an army “…like the one you have lost…” and then spell it out: horse for horse and chariot for chariot. It's a copy of the old army, just on a new battlefield. Nobody says anything about making it bigger or fancier.
The answer is False. The text says, “…the king approved their plan and acted accordingly.” Ben-hadad is king of Aram, and the plan comes from his servants. He approves it and acts on it.
The answer is Aphek. Verse 26 says Ben-hadad mobilized the Arameans and went up to Aphek to fight against Israel. Remember that name, friends, because Aphek comes back later in this very passage.

The answer is that the Aramean army covers the countryside. The Israelites camp like two small flocks of goats, while the Arameans cover the countryside. Count that gap, friends. A couple of little flocks on one side and the whole landscape on the other.

The answer is that the LORD will deliver their great army into Ahab's hand. The man of God says, “This is what the LORD says: ‘Because the Arameans have said that the LORD is a god of the hills and not of the valleys, I will deliver all this great army into your hand.’” The Arameans said it, and the LORD answers it. He gives the whole great army to Ahab, Israel's king.
The answer is that He is the LORD. The LORD says, “Then you will know that I am the LORD.” This victory is about who He is. It's not a pat on the back for anybody's army.

The answer is True. After seven days of camping across from each other, the battle ensues on the seventh day. Israel strikes down the Arameans, a hundred thousand foot soldiers in one day (1 Kings 20:29).
The answer is room, friends. Ben-hadad, king of Aram, fled to the city of Aphek and hid in an inner room (1 Kings 20:30). He's hidden away inside the city.
The answer is that they are merciful. Ben-hadad's servants say, “…we have heard that the kings of the house of Israel are merciful.” That's their hope, and they build a whole plan on it.

The answer is False. The servants say, “Let us go out to the king of Israel with sackcloth around our waists and ropes around our heads.” They don't dress for battle. They want Ahab to spare Ben-hadad's life (1 Kings 20:31).

The answer is that they quickly grab hold of that word. The men were looking for a sign of hope, and they quickly grasped at the word brother. Then they answered, “Yes, your brother Ben-hadad.” They didn't waste a second.

The answer is True, and it's a surprise. Ben-hadad, king of Aram, comes out, and Ahab has him come up into his chariot (1 Kings 20:33). A king who was hiding in an inner room is now up in the chariot of Ahab, Israel's king.

The answer is that Ahab makes a treaty and sends him away. Ahab says, “By this treaty I release you…” Then the text says, “So he made a treaty with him and sent him away.” Keep that in mind, friends, because the story isn't done with this decision.
The answer is False. One of the sons of the prophets says to his companion, “Strike me, please!” and the text says, “…the man refused to strike him.” That refusal matters in the very next verse.

The answer is that he has not obeyed the voice of the LORD. The prophet says, “Because you have not obeyed the voice of the LORD, as soon as you depart from me a lion will kill you.” It's a heavy moment, friends. The request came by the word of the LORD, and the companion didn't do it.
The answer is True. The prophet finds another man and says, “Strike me, please!” This time, “…the man struck him and wounded him…” That's the opposite of what the first man did.
The answer is a bandage over his eyes. The prophet is wounded and waits on the road for the king, so a bandage fits the part. Disguises don't get much simpler than that.

The answer is a talent of silver. The man tells the prophet, “Guard this man! If he goes missing for any reason, your life will be exchanged for his life, or you will weigh out a talent of silver.” That was the warning in the story the prophet tells Ahab.
The answer is False. Ahab answers the prophet, “So shall your judgment be; you have pronounced it on yourself.” He doesn't say free. He says the judgment stands.

The answer is the man God had devoted to destruction. The word from the LORD is, “Because you have let slip from your hand the man I had devoted to destruction…” The prophet's story was about a captive. Now we hear what it was really about.

The answer is Ahab's people for Ben-hadad's people. The LORD says, “…your life will be exchanged for his life, and your people for his people.” It's heavy, friends. The word is about more than Ahab alone.

The answer is sullen and angry. Ahab, Israel's king, heard the word from the LORD and went home to Samaria sullen and angry (1 Kings 20:43). I think that's a king who heard something he didn't want to hear.
